INTRODUCTION AND
INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE
Massachusetts, New Jersey , Arizona, California,
Colorado, the District of Columbia, Delaware, Hawai‘i,
Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New
Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont,
and Washington share strong governmental interests
in protecting public safety and preventing crime.  In
furtherance of those interests, Amici submit this brief
to explain why Cook County’s and Connecticut’s
regulation of the sale and possession of assault
weapons such as the AR-15 within their own borders
is wholly consistent with the Second Amendment.
There are few interests more important to States
than protecting public safety, and especially “the
suppression of violent crime and vindication of its
victims.” United States v. Morrison, 529 U.S. 598, 618
(2000). Amici bear a solemn responsibility: to keep our
residents safe in the public and private spaces that are
part of the fabric of daily life in a free and democratic
society. To that end, Amici enact and enforce laws that
protect the health, safety, and security of our
residents, including by ta king steps to prevent mass
shootings and other forms of gun violence that imperil
the safety of our residents and inhibit their exercise of
constitutionally protected freedoms.
Using their police powers in service of these goals,
Amici have adopted a range of measures that regulate
weapons and weapon accessories, while ensuring their
residents have access to weapons for individual selfdefense. These measures include laws that restrict
particularly lethal weapons that pose a disproportionate threat to public safety. A number of Amici
have prohibited the purchase and possession of certain

2

semiautomatic assault weapons, 1 just as the federal
government did from 1994 to 2004. 2 Although state
definitions of the prohibited class of weapons differ,
they typically encompass weapons like AR-15 and AK-
47-style rifles that inflict catastrophic injuries and
have distinct combat capabilities, rendering them
uniquely devastating in mass shootings.3 Many States
and jurisdictions have also enacted laws prohibiting or
restricting other unusually dangerous weapons,
including automatic-fire machine guns, 4 short-barreled shotguns and rifles, 5 high-caliber rifles, 6 guns
hidden in canes and other covert weapons, 7 and
grenades, rocket launchers, and other hand-held
destructive devices.8 Those laws are central to Amici’s
efforts to protect public safety.
Amici share the conviction that the Constitution
allows States—consistent with our Nation’s historical
tradition—to adopt these types of targeted protections
against gun violence in a manner adapted to their local
needs. For centuries now, States have exercised their
police powers to protect th e public from unusually
dangerous weapons that pose a disproportionate
danger to public safety. Amici have a strong interest
in ensuring that States retain their longstanding

constitutional authority to do so “with reasonable
firearms regulations” that are consistent with the
Second Amendment. McDonald v. City of Chicago, 561

today, as “dramatic technological changes” in firearms
have forced governments across the country to grapple
with “unprecedented” threats to public safety.
NYSRPA v. Bruen , 597 U.S. 1, 27 (2022). In confronting these novel threats, Amici must be able to
protect their residents by imposing measured restrictions on unusually dangerou s weapons, including
assault weapons built from the AR-15 platform.9
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Since the earliest days of the Republic, States have
regulated unusually dangerous weapons that have
contributed disproportionately to serious public safety
threats. The regulation of assault weapons fits easily
within that longstanding historical tradition.
I. From English common law to the Founding to
Reconstruction, governments have consistently
regulated weapons that are unusually dangerous—
even when the danger of those weapons was clear only
after they were widely ow ned. That well-established
regulatory tradition dates back to medieval England
and has persisted throughout American history.
That historical tradition amply justifies Cook
County’s and Connecticut’s measured restrictions on
assault weapons like the AR-15. Like other similar
laws, the challenged restrictions preserve the right of
law-abiding, responsible citizens to use firearms for
self-defense while targeting a narrow subset of

9 Subsequent references in this brief to the “AR-15” are a
shorthand for assault weapons built from the AR-15 platform.

4

weapons that pose a disproportionate risk to public
safety.
II. Petitioners’ circulation-based common use test
would grant inviolable Second Amendment protection
to any weapon that reaches an arbitrary popularity
threshold and reduce the Second Amendment to a
mere counting exercise. That test should be rejected
because it is ahistoric al, results in unqualified
protections for machineguns, is inconsistent with this
Court’s interpretation of other rights, creates an
illogical arms race between firearms manufacturers
and legislatures, and runs counter to this Court’s
recent Second Amendment decisions.
ARGUMENT
I. Regulation of Assault Weapons Falls Well
Within Our Historical Tradition.
This Court has repeatedly affirmed that courts
reviewing firearm regulations must evaluate them
based on the “principles that underpin our regulatory
tradition.” Wolford v. Lopez, 609 U.S. 185, 198 (2026)
(quoting United States v. Rahimi, 602 U.S. 680, 692
(2024)). Given “dramatic technological changes” in
firearms that have precipitated “unprecedented”
threats to public safety, NYSRPA v. Bruen , 597 U.S.
1, 27 (2022), these principles “can[] and must” be
identified broadly enough that States may address
“circumstances beyond those the Founders specifically
anticipated,” United States v. Hemani , 608 U.S. 772,
783 (2026) (quoting Bruen, 597 U.S. at 28). Otherwise,
courts risk “trapp[ing]” the law “in amber” and
depriving States of their constitutional authority
when the People seek to respond to the threat of mass
firearm violence. Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 691.

5

Against this backdrop, States responding to the
threat of mass shootings by regulating assault
weapons stand on solid historical ground. The
historical evidence underscores the longstanding
constitutional authority of States to protect their
residents from unusually dangerous weapons that
contribute disproportionately to serious public safety
threats. Laws regulating assault weapons are a modern application of this longstanding and diverse
tradition of regulating unusually dangerous weapons—that is, weapons whose features are disproportionately dangerous compared to their civilian selfdefense uses. That regulatory tradition dates back to
14th-century England, finds support in sources like
Blackstone, and has persisted throughout American
history. The diversity of restrictions is indicative of
how broadly this tradition sweeps.
Under any reasonable understanding of that tradition, assault weapons are disproportionately dangerous compared to their civilian self-defense uses.
Assault weapons like the AR-15 were designed to kill
armored enemy combatants in offensive battlefield
situations. They are rarely used in real-world selfdefense situations. But they are used with increasing
frequency in the deadliest mass shootings across the
Nation. State and local laws restricting assault
weapons like the AR-15 thus comport fully with the
principles underlying our Nation’s historical tradition
of firearms regulation.
A. Under Our Historical Tradition, States
Can Regulate Unusually Dangerous
Weapons That Contribute Disproportionately to a Public Safety Problem.
Our nation has a long historical tradition of
regulating unusually dangerous weapons. A “variety

6

of sources,” including “historical analogues,” “scholarship,” and this Court’s own precedent, support that
conclusion. Wolford, 609 U.S. at 196. From before the
Founding to the present, State legislatures have
consistently regulated unusually dangerous weapons,
including launcegays, crossbows, hagbuts, trap guns,
slungshots, clubs, pistols, machineguns,
semiautomatic firearms, and Bowie knives. They have
done so on the ground that, despite their popular
appeal for ostensibly lawfu l purposes, these weapons
nonetheless disproportionately threaten public safety.
This evidence “confirm[s] what common sense
suggests”: States are not powerless to respond to the
growing public safety threat posed by mass shootings.
Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 698. Togeth er with the fact that
States are facing public-safety threats “that could not
have arisen when the Second or Fourteenth
Amendment was adopted,” Wolford, 609 U.S. at 197,
the historical record underscores the broad tradition
of regulating disproportionately dangerous weapons.
1. The historical record underscores that there is a
longstanding tradition of regulating unusually
dangerous weapons. “From the earliest days of the
common law, firearm regulations have included
provisions barring people from misusing weapons to
harm or menace others.” Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 693.
Regulations like the 1328 Statute of Northampton
codified the common-law rule that “go[ing] armed to
terrify the King’s subjects” was a “great offence.” Id.10

10 The United States suggests that Englishmen were exempt
from these laws if they carried common weapons. See US.Br.11
(quoting 1 William Hawkins, A Treatise of the Pleas of the Crown
136 (1716)). But the citation says that “Persons of Quality are in
no Danger of Offending against this Statute by wearing common

7

But the Statute of Northampton did not apply only to
conduct; it also prohibited dangerous weapons like
“the launcegay,” a “10- to 12-foot-long lightweight
lance” often used to “breach the peace.” Bruen, 597
U.S. at 41. So even before the Founding, the government regulated particularly dangerous weapons in
addition to conduct.
Beyond prohibitions on particular weapons, “going
armed” laws also made it “a  crime against the public
peace” to carry “dangerous  or unusual weapons” to
“terrify[] the good peop le of the land.” William
Blackstone, 4 Commentaries on the Laws of England
55, 149 (1769). That reference to “dangerous or
unusual weapons” was a hendiadys, a “figure of speech
in which two terms, separa ted by a conjunction, are
melded together to form a single complex expression.”
Samuel Bray, “Necessary and Proper” and “Cruel and
Unusual”: Hendiadys in the Constitution, 102 V A. L.
REV. 687, 695 (2016). And given their familiarity with
hendiadyses, “[e]ducated readers in the Founding era
would have interpreted [dangerous or unusual
weapons]” to be “a ban on weapons that were
‘unusually dangerous.’” Nat’l Ass’n for Gun Rts. v.

Weapons, or having their usual Number of Attendants with them
for their Ornament or Defence.” Hawkins, at 136 (emphasis
added). Because “Persons of Quality” simply meant nobility, this
“exemption was a categorical privilege of class and rank,”
recognized because nobility traveling “did not produce a ‘terror to
the people.’” Saul Cornell, History, Text, Tradition, and the
Future of Second Amendment Jurisprudence: Limits on Armed
Travel Under Anglo-American Law, 1688-1868, 83 L. & CONTEMP.
PROBS. 73, 84–85 (2020). The law that applied to the vast majority
of the country, and thus informs our understanding of the right,
did not hinge on the commonality of the weapon.

8

Lamont (“NAGR”), 153 F.4th 213, 233 (2d Cir. 2025).11
That broad allowance for regulating unusually dangerous
weapons tracks closely the Statute of Northampton’s
prohibition on launcegays and  bespeaks a regulatory
framework designed to mitigate the public safety
threat posed by unusually dangerous weapons.
That tradition continued through the 1689 English
Bill of Rights, a “predecessor” to the Second
Amendment, which secured for certain Englishmen
the right to “have Arms for their Defence suitable to
their Conditions, and as allowed by Law.”  District of
Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570, 593 (2008) (quoting
1 W. & M., c. 2, §7, in 3 Eng. Stat. at Large 441 (1689)).
Scholars of the time recognized that, despite the broad
right, the Crown could still “restrain the use of some

11 Many Founding-era sources used “dangerous or unusual”
interchangeably with “dangerous and unusual,” NAGR, 153
F.4th at 233 & n.18; compare Heller, 554 U.S. at 627 (“dangerous
and unusual weapons”), with id. at 623 (“dangerous or unusual
weapons”), and Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 697 (same), demonstrating
that this was not a simple conjunc tive or disjunctive test giving
each word its dictionary meaning. Indeed, a test that treats
“dangerous” and “unusual” as two separate inquiries makes little
sense. All arms are dangerous, so  a test where “dangerous” is
dispositive would encompass all firearms. See Hanson v. District
of Columbia, 120 F.4th 223, 238 n.7 (D.C. Cir. 2024) (per curiam).
And a test where “unusual” is dispositive hinges entirely on
popularity, particularly if read to refer to numerical availability
instead of conveying some heightened level of lethality. See
NAGR, 153 F.4th at 233. Instead, the best reading of this
phrase—both historically and linguistically—is that it contemplates the regulation of unusually dangerous weapons. See
NAGR, 153 F.4th at 234 n.19; Hanson, 120 F.4th at 238 n.7.
“‘[D]angerous’ needs a modifier and its companion ‘unusual’
needs something to modify.” NAGR, 153 F.4th at 234. So as Judge
Walker on the Second Circuit rightly concluded, “ [u]nusually
dangerous is the obvious fit.” Id.

9

particular sort of arms.” Granville Sharp, Tracts,
Concerning the Ancient and Only True Legal Means of
National Defence, by a Free Militia 17–18 (1782). And
the Crown exercised that authority to regulate
weapons—like “cross-bows” and “hagbuts”—that were
particularly dangerous, had little value in selfdefense, and were likely to “favour the designs of
murderers.” Id. at 18.
This “ancient common law tradition of singling out
weapons capable of producing a terror” not only
persisted in English law for centuries; it also traveled
with the colonists across the Atlantic. NAGR, 153
F.4th at 246. For that reason, state legislatures in the
18th and 19th centuries “passed laws in a number of
states that restricted the use or ownership of certain
types of weapons once it became obvious that those
weapons” threatened public  safety, especially by
“contributing to rising crime rates.” Bianchi v. Brown,
111 F.4th 438, 468 (4th Ci r. 2024) (en banc). That
historical evidence, which involves restrictions on
several different types of weapons, underscores the
broad authority of States to regulate unusually
dangerous weapons. Four prominent examples are
illustrative:
Trap Guns. These weapons involved “the rigging of
a firearm to discharge when a person unwittingly trips
a string or wire.” Duncan v. Bonta, 133 F.4th 852, 875
(9th Cir. 2025) (en banc). Although they were
“popular” in the early days of the Republic, id., it
quickly became clear that widespread use of trap guns
resulted in the death of innocent civilians. New Jersey
criminalized their usage in 1771, finding that they
were “most dangerous” and “too much prevailed in this
Province.” 1763–1775 N.J. Laws 346, ch. 539, § 10.
Other States followed suit, with nine “bann[ing] the

10

setting of trap guns in the 18th and 19th centuries.”
Duncan, 133 F.4th at 875.
Bowie Knives.  Bowie knives are a “leading
example” of the longstanding tradition of regulating
unusually dangerous weapons. Barnett v. Raoul , 180
F.4th 1035, 1047 (7th Cir. 2026). These 19th-century
arms “were technological advancements over ordinary
defensive arms” of the time “because they were
designed ‘expressly for fighting,’ with longer blades,
crossguards to protect fighters’ hands, and clip points
to facilitate cutting or stabbing adversaries.” NAGR,
153 F.4th at 243; see also Knife Rights, Inc. v. Bonta ,
165 F.4th 1330, 1343 (9th Cir. 2026). Thanks to their
design, these weapons were used in “widely-publicized
act[s] of violence resulting in multiple fatalities” and
“an alarming proportion of the era’s murders and
serious assaults.” NAGR, 153 F.4th at 243.
“[W]hen the country experienced a ‘nationwide
surge of homicides’ in the nineteenth century, states
reacted by ‘passing laws severely restricting access’”
to, among other “dangerous weapons,” the popularly
owned Bowie knife. Ocean State Tactical, LLC v.
Rhode Island, 95 F.4th 38, 48 (1st Cir. 2024) (“ OST”).
These “ubiquitous historical restrictions,” NAGR, 153
F.4th at 243, appeared in “forty-nine states and the
District of Columbia” when “their popularity in the
hands of murderers became apparent,” OST, 95 F.4th
at 46. The laws “ranged from outright bans on their
manufacture, sale, and possession; to enhanced
criminal penalties for those who used the weapons to
commit crimes; to prohibitions on both open and
concealed carry.” Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 467; see also id
at n.5 (collecting citations); Hanson v. District of
Columbia, 120 F.4th 223, 237 (D.C. Cir. 2024) (per
curiam) (reiterating that some States “ban[ned] the

11

carrying, rather than only the concealment, of Bowie
knives with no or narrow exceptions” and collecting
citations).
Restrictions on Bowie knives were prevalent even
though these knives were commonplace and were not
used for criminal ends alone. In the 19th century,
these weapons had become “widespread” and were
sometimes “used for lawful purposes” like self-defense
and hunting before they were restricted. Barnett, 180
F.4th at 1047–48. Indeed, Bowie knives were a
“common part of Americ an life” in the 1800s. Id.
(quoting David B. Kopel, Clayton E. Cramer & Joseph
Edward Olson, Knives and the Second Amendment, 47
U. MICH. J.L. REFORM 167, 184 (2013)). They were
“widely carried by Americans of all stripes,” including
“‘upstanding citizens and villains’ alike.” Id. at 1047
(quoting Norm Flayderman, The Bowie Knife:
Unsheathing an American Legend 20, 125, 130 (2004)).
In fact, they were so popular that “European visitors
who ventured beyond the Appalachians found [the
Bowie knife] such an integral part of the American
way of life that they felt compelled to comment on it at
length in accounts of their adventures.” Id. (quoting
Harold L. Peterson, American Knives: The First
History and Collectors’ Guide 25 (1958)) (alteration in
original).
Nonetheless, restrictions on Bowie knives
repeatedly survived legal challenges, with several
“[c]ontemporaneous court decisions” upholding “laws
targeting Bowie knives against challenges based upon
the Second Amendment or a state equivalent.”
Hanson, 120 F.4th at 238. In upholding restrictions on
Bowie knives, the Tennessee Supreme Court looked
specifically to their comparative capacity for violence
against civilians, explaining that the knives were

12

“usually employed in private broils,” “efficient only in
the hands of the robber and the assassin,” and “could
not be employed advantag eously in the common
defense of the citizen”—despite their obvious
popularity and capacity to stave off attackers. Aymette
v. State, 21 Tenn. 154, 158 (1840). The Texas Supreme
Court agreed that “[t]he Bowie Knife differs from
[guns or swords] in its device and design: it is the
instrument of almost certain death.” Cockrum v. State,
24 Tex. 394, 402 (1859). It explained that “[h]e who
carries such a weapon,” even ostensibly “for lawful
defense,” “makes himself more dangerous to the rights
of others.” Id.  at 403;  see also id. (referring to the
Bowie knife as “the most deadly of all weapons in
common use”); Haynes v. Tennessee, 24 Tenn. 120, 122
(1844) (noting Bowie knives were “extremely
dangerous and destructive to human life”); State v.
Workman, 35 W. Va. 367, 373 (1891) (holding that
Bowie knives are not protected by the Second
Amendment). These cases make clear that the
weapon’s capacity for carnage, not its rarity, was what
rendered it “uncommon.”
The United States incorrectly suggests that state
courts endorsed the regulation of Bowie knives
because they were “not in common use” and were
instead employed primarily for criminal ends.
US.Br.12–14. That assertion cannot be squared with
the historical evidence described above, which
demonstrates the ubiquity of Bowie-knife use for
lawful purposes. The special danger posed by Bowie
knives, rather than any lack of popularity with the
public, explains why 19th-century courts refused to
treat Bowie knives as “usual arms.” See NAGR, 153
F.4th at 243 (“In certain respects, [Bowie] knives were
superior even to contemporary firearms, which had
limited effectiveness in close quarters.”); Barnett, 180

13

F.4th at 1047 (contrasting the Bowie knife’s ease of
repeated use with a key “technological shortcoming” of
the “era’s prominent firearms”: the cumbersome need
to reload).
Meanwhile, Petitioners raise the Georgia Supreme
Court’s decision in Nunn v. State , 1 Ga. 243 (1846),
Pet.Br.47, which struck down “an ambiguous statute”
insofar as it “prohibited open carry” of Bowie knives.
Barnett, 180 F.4th at 1049. But as Judge St. Eve
explained in Barnett, courts should not “place on Nunn
more weight than it can be ar,” particularly given
Nunn’s legal infirmities and limited adoption
elsewhere. Id. Nunn says that the Second Amendment
protects the “right to bear arms of every description.”
1 Ga. at 251. As Judge Richardson observed in
Bianchi, that holding implies that the “Second
Amendment does not permit the banning of any
weapons,” which is “inconsistent with the
overwhelming authority to the contrary.” Bianchi, 111
F.4th at 513 n.47 (Richardson, J., dissenting); see
Heller, 554 U.S. at 626 (“From Blackstone through the
19th-century cases, commentators and courts
routinely explained that the right was not a right to
keep and carry any weapon whatsoever in any manner
whatsoever and for whatever purpose.”). Bruen
instructs courts not to give “disproportionate weight”
to outlier cases that “c ontradict[] the overwhelming
majority of other evidence.” 597 U.S. at 65–66. That
applies to Nunn, which “is an outlier of little value in
discerning the nature of ‘dangerous and unusual’
weapons in the Anglo-American legal tradition.”
Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 513 n.47 (Richardson, J.,
dissenting).
Slungshots. These weapons, which were comprised
of “a weight fastened to the end of a chain or rope that

14

can be swung around to apply blunt force to an
opponent,” were, like Bowie knives, “particularly
suitable for fighting.” Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 467 & n.9.
Given their particular dangerousness, “[r]estrictions
on slungshots were more severe and widespread than
restrictions on other excessively dangerous weapons,”
and many States outright banned their “sale and
possession.” Id. at 467 n.9. By the end of the 19th
century, “nearly every State had enacted antislungshot laws.” Duncan, 133 F.4th at 876; see also,
e.g., 1850 Mass. Acts & Resolves 401, 401 (making it a
crime to “manufacture, or cause to be manufactured,
or sell, or expose for sale, any instrument or weapon of
the kind usually known as a slung shot”); 1868 Fla.
Laws 95, Of Offenses Against the Public Peace, ch. 7,
§ 11; 1881 Ill. Crim. Code 73, Regulating the Traffic in
Deadly Weapons, § 1; 1885 Minn. Penal Code, Title 12,
Of Crimes Against the Public Health and Safety
§§ 333-334; 1890 Okla. Sess. Laws 475, ch. 25, art. 38,
§ 18.
Machineguns and semiautomatic firearms.
Semiautomatic firearms “became available to
consumers in the 1890s,” and “automatic weapons
quickly followed.” Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 469. Civilian
use of automatic weapons led to “a different type of
homicide”: “mass murder spurred by the commercial
availability of weaponry that empowered individuals
to kill many people quickly.” Id. at 468. And, as with
other weapons, “their use in multiple-fatality
homicides and terror” led to regulation, including the
“National Firearms Act of 1934, which prohibited
ownership of machine guns, submachine guns, and
short-barreled shotguns.” NAGR, 153 F.4th at 245–46.
That Act followed the 29 states which had already
enacted “anti-machine-gun laws between 1925 and

15

1934.” Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 470; see id.  at nn.14–15
(collecting statutes).
*  *  *
Drawing on the historical evidence—from the
Statute of Northampton to the National Firearms Act
and beyond—six circuits have identified a tradition of

2. The widespread agreement among the circuits—
based on multiple historical analogues—is reinforced
by this Court’s recent precedents explaining how to
appropriately define the relevant historical tradition.

16

For one thing, while this Court has acknowledged
that a party defending firearm regulations may “rely
on” either “a single analogue or a group of analogues,”
it has made clear that a regulatory tradition derived
from multiple historical analogues (as here) sweeps
more broadly than those traditions defined by a single
historical legal regime. Wolford, 609 U.S. at 196. That
principle is clear from Rahimi. There, the Court
identified a tradition of disarming those “who threaten
physical harm to others from misusing firearms” by
relying on “two distinct legal regimes”: surety and
affray laws. 602 U.S. at 690, 694–95. The Court
recognized that the statute at issue was “by no means
identical to these founding era regimes”; neither
analogue disarmed dangerous persons, let alone
focused specifically on domestic violence. Id. at 698.
Nonetheless, the Court identified a common purpose
of “address[ing] firearms violence” by individuals who
“pose[] a clear threat of ph ysical violence to another”
(the “why”). Id. at 694. And because the tradition itself
included various approaches to regulating firearm
usage by dangerous individuals (the “how”), the Court
held that the modern law—although certainly without
any historical twin—“fit[] neatly” into the relevant
tradition, id. at 698, when defined at the “right level
of generality,” id. at 740 (Barrett, J., concurring).
By contrast, Wolford and Hemani show how a
comparatively sparse historical record leads to a more
limited definition of the relevant historical traditions.
In both cases, the Court seriously considered only one
single set of regulations. See Wolford, 609 U.S. at 208
(noting that the State’s main argument relies “almost
entirely” on “laws that prohibited unauthorized
hunting”); Hemani, 608 U.S. at 781 (observing that the
government relies on “habitual drunkard laws”). So
the Court’s analysis focused on a narrower “how” and

17

“why” undergirding those specific laws, making it
more challenging for the government to place its
modern restrictions within the relevant tradition.
Wolford, 609 U.S. at 208–10.
It therefore follows that where a historical tradition
draws from multiple historical analogues, the
tradition should be defined at a higher level of
generality. If a historical legislature dealt with a
discrete issue—like unauthorized hunting on private
lands—it is difficult to show that a distinct, if similar,
modern tradition shares a “how” and a “why.” By
contrast, if multiple historical legislatures repeatedly
addressed the same issue at different times and in
different ways, it is more likely that a law which is not
“identical” to any of its forebearers nonetheless
comports with a general historical principle that
connects those various historical analogues. Rahimi,
602 U.S. at 698. In other words, when there are
multiple historical analogues that form the basis for a
historical tradition, modern regulatory approaches
(the “how”) to addressing the same overarching
problems (the “why”) are more likely to be “consistent
with [the] right,” and it is far less likely that any
specific historical law perfectly demarcates the outer
limits of state authority. Wolford, 609 U.S. at 196.
That principle applies here. States have taken
multiple historical approaches to addressing the
misuse of unusually dangerous weapons. So modern
regulatory approaches to addressing that same
overarching problem are more likely to fit comfortably
within the historical tradition.
To be clear, courts should not assume that a prior
legislature’s inaction implies an absence of authority.
See Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 739–40 (Barrett, J.,
concurring) (rejecting “a ‘use it or lose it’ view of

18

legislative authority”). The Constitution does not
require States to legislate to the zenith of their
authority by, for example, restricting novel weapons
that have yet to pose a public safety problem. The
Second Amendment, like the First Amendment, allows
States the flexibility to “adopt laws to address the
problems that confront them.” McCullen v. Coakley ,
573 U.S. 464, 481 (2014).
The “distinctively modern” nature of mass-shootings
provides yet another reason to define the historical
tradition broadly. Wolford , 609 U.S. at 198. Since
Bruen, this Court has recognized that cases “implycating unprecedented societal concerns or dramatic
technological changes may require” courts to define
the relevant traditions at higher levels of generality.
597 U.S. at 27–28. That “more nuanced approach,” id.,
is triggered not only when  social or technological
change presents a novel issue, but also when our
understanding of the problem has changed with time,
as Rahimi underscored. After all, women have “feared
[] domestic violence” since the Founding. Rahimi, 602
U.S. at 763 (Thomas, J., dissenting). But it is not until
relatively recently that legislatures have intervened to
handle the “potentially deadly combination” of
“[f]irearms and domestic strife.” Voisine v. United
States, 579 U.S. 686, 689 (2016). So as in Rahimi, this
Court should define the relevant historical tradition at
a higher level of generality when the legislature is
responding to new manifestations of a longstanding
harm. See also Wolford, 609 U.S. at 198.
In other words, whether this Court understands
mass shootings as a new threat or a new manifestation
of longstanding concerns about firearm violence, “[t]he
dramatic technological change embodied in AR-15s
equipped with large-capacity magazines” has fueled

19

the “unprecedented societal concern of mass killings

Although multi-casualty murders did occur in the

The restrictions at issue in this case fit comfortably

Still, in describing the underlying principles, this

II. Petitioners’ Circulation-Based Test Cannot Be Squared With Historical Tradition
or Modern Reality.

supporting the regulation of unusually dangerous
weapons, Petitioners claim that any firearm “in
common use” is “protected by the Second Amendment”
and thus beyond a State’s authority to regulate.
Pet.Br.34. That position—which reduces the Second
Amendment to a mere counting exercise—should be

civilian hands “before the government can sufficiently
regulate [them].” NAGR, 153 F.4th at 233. As the First
Circuit noted, “[i]t defies reason to say that
legislatures can only ban a weapon if they ban it at (or
around) the time of its introduction.” OST, 95 F.4th at
50. Neither our historical tradition of regulating
unusually dangerous fire arms nor common sense
supports the notion that governments can regulate
firearms only if they get in the game early enough.
Fifth, Petitioners’ theory runs counter to this
Court’s Second Amendment cases. If common use were
the central inquiry, then Bruen need not have
proceeded beyond the statement that no “party
dispute[s] that handguns are weapons ‘in common use’
today for self-defen se.” 597 U.S. at 32. 14 Instead, this

searching historical review to assess each regulation
according to our history. And in line with longstanding
tradition, the Amendment “do[es] not shield popular
weapons from review of their potentially unusually
dangerous character.” Id. Indeed, merely counting the
number of firearms in private hands does not resemble
the historical analysis this Court undertook in Heller,
Rahimi, Hemani, or Wolford. Nor does our historical
tradition support the notion—now pressed by
Petitioners—that States are powerless to stop the
spread of unusually danger ous weapons once they
reach a particular threshold level of circulation.
At bottom, Petitioners’ circulation-based test would
represent a remarkable break from history, this
Court’s precedent, and common sense. It would risk
opening the floodgates for other unusually dangerous
weapons—just because sales of those weapons have
cleared some arbitrary popularity threshold. No
matter whether this Court affirms the judgments of
the Second and Seventh Circuits, it should reject
Petitioners’ ahistorical Second Amendment test.
